To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Whole-genome sequencing (WGSe) and whole-exomic sequencing (WESe) can be used for cancer diagnostics, but are not yet ready for clinical use.

1) the application of NGS-based diagnostics in the clinic is a promising approach to identify the best available treatment for the individual patient; 2) the clinical evidence of NGS-based diagnostic is not yet sufficient for decision-making in the clinic; 3) the application of the NGS technology in the clinic requires a new paradigm of clinical evidence and a new approach to clinical trials; 4) the NGS-based diagnostics will be an important tool for the future of personalized cancer medicine.

(a) WGS and WES are feasible in a clinical setting and provide a comprehensive landscape of somatic and inherited variants in a single run; (b) the majority of variants detected by WES are also detected by WGS and vice versa; and (c) the number of variants identified is not the only parameter for the selection of the best available sequencing approach.
